summary: I built a page-level replay of campaign 34's SSD tier (page chains from the trace's block ids, writes from the client records checked against h2s_submit, lookups from s2h_query, the logged cleaner passes) and it reproduces the run: for ec_full all 9,103 lookups, all 10 reads that failed on a deleted file and all 17,095 requests' cached tokens match the logs (jit_exact 8,361 of 8,363 lookups, jit_p50 8,554 of 8,566). Today's order (oldest written first) deletes 7,038 live pages in three passes before 6,600 s, 6,793 of them held by two or more sessions; after the first pass 59 of about 2,880 requests recompute 1.21 M tokens (101 lookups find nothing, 13 find part, 7 reads fail), and every lookup that found nothing lost a page another session had written. By N g that is 1.6 to 1.9 s of mean TTFT in minutes 90 to 110 across the three arms (inferred through the identity, on the recorded timeline). Section 4.3's 'ended sessions' chains first' is wrong as written: setting an ended session's whole chain to time zero makes it worse (3.6 to 4.0 s), because 94.5 % of pages shared across sessions sit in first prompts and 60 % of the shared tokens new sessions find were held only by sessions already over. Zeroing only the ended session's pages past its first prompt leaves 0.17 to 0.25 s. Refreshing a chain's file times at each request leaves 0.07 to 0.13 s and needs 952 pages (1,904 file touches) a second, or 216 pages a second at one refresh per session per 300 s with the same result; touching only what a lookup finds (283 pages a second) does as well at this volume. Both together leave 0.00 to 0.03 s; the oracle leaves nothing at any volume tested, so dead pages are always enough and the problem is only telling them apart. At half the volume today's order costs 2.7 to 3.7 s and at a quarter 8.0 to 8.8 s, where sessions also lose heads they wrote themselves; a three-class order (ended tails first, ended first prompts next, open sessions by last use) holds 0.05 to 0.06 s and 0.74 to 0.98 s, and 0.40 to 0.46 s at a quarter with reference counts over open sessions' chains. No loss in the replay needs an in-memory index of stored pages: what remains is first use by a session of pages whose last holder had ended, which an index cannot foresee, and a per-page use count changed the result by 3 % or less. The replay is open loop, so it cannot show how less recompute would change the queue; nothing in the engine was changed.

findings.question: Step 1: does the page-level replay reproduce what happened in campaign 34 (lookups after each pass that found nothing or part, reads that failed, tokens recomputed)?
findings.answer: Yes. Trace reconstruction: the client's ideal_cached is reproduced for 17,095 of 17,095 ec_full requests. Write model: 31.56 M tokens against 31.60 M in h2s_submit, within 0.03 to 0.08 % per 10 minutes; a write is done a median 0.05 to 0.55 s after the client's prefill end. Volume: 390,100 pages (25.0 M tokens) at 100 %; a pass at the first 30 s tick at or over 90 %, down to 80 %, lands within 2 s of each logged pass and within 100 groups (40,450/39,800/39,550/42,150 against 40,400/39,850/39,650/42,200). ec_full with the logged passes: every one of 9,103 lookups gets its logged hit (5,852 before pass 1; after it 141 found nothing, 24 part, 1,332 all, 1,754 asked only new text), all 10 failed reads fail, all 17,095 requests end with the recorded cached tokens. Per interval, logged = replay: pass 1 to 2: 49 lookups found nothing, 2 part, 505 all, 5 reads failed, 1,516 requests recomputed 639.5 K tokens (61.8 K with nothing deleted), 25 requests lost 1,024 tokens or more; pass 2 to 3: 49 / 9 / 435, 3 reads failed, 543.4 K (14.8 K), 30 requests; pass 3 to 4: 41 / 13 / 386, 1 read failed; after pass 4: 2 / 0 / 1. jit_exact: 8,361 of 8,363 lookups, 11 of 12 failed reads, 17,113 of 17,114 requests; jit_p50: 8,554 of 8,566, 9 of 9, 17,048 of 17,049 (the misses are staged reads of the planned chain). The passes deleted file times up to 771, 1,314, 1,853 and 2,492 s, i.e. pages older than 75 to 79 minutes. Unlinks happen in the last 7 % or so of a pass: lookups at 0.17 to 0.90 of a pass still found the oldest files, one at 0.97 did not.
findings.method: /home/wanhr/sglang/agent_cache/results/design_unified_1126/agents/ev_ssd/: c34lib.py (chains), replay.py (store, lookups, reads, cleaner), check_ideal.py, check_writes.py, check_wtime.py, validate.py -> out/validate_<arm>.out, reproduce.py -> out/reproduce_<arm>.txt, passwin.py -> out/passwin.out. Inputs: extracts/<arm>.evt (grep of the three server logs), each arm's client.jsonl, extracts/trees_c34.jsonl.gz (the 678 trees played). Code facts re-read at HEAD: nixl_cleaner.py:168-223 and :270, hicache_nixl.py:645-664 and :853-875, nixl_utils.py:320-333, nixl_registry.py:152-153 (reads open files read-only), cache_controller.py:1061-1076 and :1103-1147, hicache_storage.py:23.
findings.implication: The replay can be used to compare cleaning orders on the recorded timeline. It is open loop: send times, in-memory prefixes and the lookups each request makes are the recorded ones.

findings.question: What does today's order (a, oldest written first) lose, and through which pages?
findings.answer: ec_full at the run's volume: three passes before 6,600 s delete 119,800 pages, 7,038 of them live (a later request's prompt holds them), 6,793 of those held by two or more sessions; the first pass deletes 3,323 live pages of 40,450, all shared. From the first pass (5,263 s) to 6,600 s: 101 lookups find nothing, 13 find part, 7 reads fail; 59 of about 2,880 requests recompute 1.21 M tokens beyond a store that deletes nothing (jit_exact 60 requests, 1.21 M; jit_p50 52, 0.97 M). 57 of the 59 lose through a page held by two or more sessions; in all 41 requests whose lookup found nothing the missing page was last written by another session (none by the session itself); 23 of the 59 are first requests of new sessions (142 K tokens), which the review's scripts did not count. By N g with N = 128 and 0.043 ms a token: 2.31 s over the 22 minutes after the first pass; in minutes 90 to 110, 0.90 / 0.82 / 0.77 M tokens and 1.91 / 1.70 / 1.63 s (ec_full / jit_exact / jit_p50); with the measured 0.73 N it would be 27 % less.
findings.method: compare.py <arm> 1.0 0.90 0.80 -> out/cmp_<arm>_1.0_0.90_0.80.txt and out/compare_<arm>_s1_90_80.json (order a_oldest_written, volume model); mechanisms.py -> out/mechanisms_<arm>_s1_90_80.txt; losses.py -> out/losses_ec_full_s1.txt. A loss is counted against a replay in which nothing is deleted, so lookup-cap and re-eviction losses are excluded.
findings.implication: Section 4.3's sentence 'today's cleaner deletes the oldest-written page first, which is the shared head' holds at page level at this volume. The TTFT figure is inferred through the closed-loop identity; the recorded late TTFT is 27 to 28 s, so the cleaner is about 6 to 7 % of it.

findings.question: (b) Ended sessions' pages first: does setting their file time to zero at the end signal help?
findings.answer: Not as written. Zeroing the ended session's whole chain: 129 requests and 2.60 M tokens after the first pass (ec_full), 3.59 / 3.59 / 3.96 s in minutes 90 to 110 against 1.91 / 1.70 / 1.63 s today. Zeroing only pages the session wrote: 3.13 to 3.32 s; sparing pages another open session's chain holds: 2.30 to 2.68 s; sparing pages a second session has used so far: 2.43 s (ec_full). Cause: 21,547 pages are held by two or more sessions and 94.5 % of them are in some session's first prompt; 506 of 695 first requests share pages with earlier sessions (2.30 M tokens) and for 242 of them (1.38 M tokens, 60 %) every earlier holder was already over. A zeroed head stays at zero when a later session uses it from memory, and equal-time files go in directory-scan order, which punches holes (102 partial chains). Zeroing only the ended session's pages past its first prompt: 7 requests, 119 K tokens, 0.17 / 0.25 / 0.20 s; 207 K of the 352 K stored pages are then at time zero at the first pass, so a 40 K pass never reaches a live page. The spread over five scan orders is 79 to 126 K tokens for this variant and 1.69 to 1.91 M for the whole-chain one.
findings.method: compare.py orders b_end_chain, b_end_own, b_end_index, b_end_private, b_end_tail; heads.py -> out/heads_ec_full.txt; tie_seeds.py -> out/tie_seeds_ec_full_1.0.txt; class sizes from pass_log in out/compare_ec_full_s1_90_80.json. End signal = the stream's last request in the trace (566 of 695 sessions; equals hint.ended in the dist-hint arms, check_end.py).
findings.implication: R1 and R4 must not mark an ended session's chain first out. The rule that works is: the ended session's pages past its first prompt go first. R1's write skip is safe on this trace: last turns of ended sessions write 1.47 M tokens (4.7 % of writes) and later sessions hold 26 K of them (out/r1_exposure_ec_full.txt).

findings.question: (c) Refreshing a chain's file times when it is used: what does it remove, and how many file touches a second does it need?
findings.answer: At the run's volume a refresh at each request's end leaves 6 requests and 62 / 36 / 31 K tokens in minutes 90 to 110: 0.13 / 0.07 / 0.07 s. It needs 952 pages a second late in the run, 1,904 file touches (two files a page), peak 1,850 pages a second over 10 s. One refresh per session per 60 s: 667 pages (1,334 files) a second; per 300 s: 216 pages (431 files) a second; the loss is the same (62 -> 63 K). Touching the head last or first makes no difference (6 against 7 requests; at a quarter volume 1,146 against 1,170 K). Touching only the pages a lookup finds (touch on read): 283 pages a second and 0.07 / 0.08 / 0.07 s at this volume; it falls behind when the volume shrinks (half: 0.61 / 0.42 / 0.44 s against 0.29 / 0.29 / 0.32 s; quarter: 3.4 to 3.8 s against 2.4 to 2.7 s). What (c) leaves at the run's volume is first requests of new sessions whose head's last user ended more than 75 minutes earlier. Rewriting a page when the touch finds no file added nothing (out/repair_ec_full_*.txt).
findings.method: compare.py orders c_refresh, c_refresh_60s, c_refresh_300s (a request ending inside the limit gets a deferred refresh when the limit expires), c_refresh_headfirst, touch_on_read, c_refresh+hit; touch rates in out/summary.txt (last block); repair.py.
findings.implication: Worth building, and the cheapest step is a touch in the lookup or read path. The review's verdict that touch-on-read would not protect shared heads does not hold at 160 GB of host memory: chains leave memory often enough that some session reads a live head from the SSD inside the 75-minute horizon. The cost of a utime call on this volume was not measured.

findings.question: (d) Both b and c, and what order works across volumes?
findings.answer: b as written plus c: 0.84 / 0.77 / 0.89 s, worse than c alone. Ended sessions' pages past the first prompt at zero plus c: 1 to 2 requests, 0.8 to 13 K tokens, 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.03 s at the run's volume, 0.05 to 0.07 s at half. At a quarter that two-class rule leaves 2.1 to 2.3 s, because recently ended sessions' first prompts are younger than idle open sessions' chains. Three classes by file time (ended sessions' pages past the first prompt at zero; ended sessions' first prompts set below every open session's page; open sessions by last refresh) give 0.00 to 0.03 s at the run's volume, 0.05 to 0.06 s at half and 0.87 / 0.98 / 0.74 s at a quarter with no index; with reference counts over open sessions' latest chains (about 60 K page keys), a touch on lookup hits and the cleaner re-checking a file's time before the unlink: 0.00, 0.04 and 0.46 / 0.41 / 0.40 s.
findings.method: compare.py orders d_chain+refresh, d_tail+refresh, d_tier+refresh, d_tier_index+refresh+hit+recheck in out/cmp_<arm>_<scale>_<hi>_<lo>.txt; tier rule in replay.py Sim.ev_end.
findings.implication: Replace section 4.3's order with the three classes. All of it is expressible through file times, as R4 proposes; the reference counts matter only below about half the run's volume.

findings.question: (e) What does an oracle (farthest next use first, never a page with a live descendant) lose?
findings.answer: Nothing: 0 requests in every setting for ec_full and jit_exact (jit_p50 at a quarter volume: 2 requests, 3.9 K tokens, from staged reads of output pages that no prompt holds). At the first pass the open sessions' latest chains are 60,661 pages (3.9 M tokens) of 352 K stored; a quarter volume keeps 78 K pages after a pass.
findings.method: compare.py orders e_oracle_next_use and e_oracle_ssd_need (next recorded SSD lookup); heads.py for live sizes.
findings.implication: Capacity is not the constraint down to a quarter of the volume. Every loss is a failure to tell dead pages from live ones, so the whole 1.6 to 1.9 s (and 8 to 9 s at a quarter) is recoverable in principle.

findings.question: Step 3: the same at half and a quarter of the volume, and with marks at 80/70?
findings.answer: TTFT at stake in minutes 90 to 110, ec_full / jit_exact / jit_p50. Marks 80/70 at the run's volume (first pass at minute 78): today 1.63 / 1.34 / 1.44 s; c 0.09 / 0.10 / 0.09; three classes plus c 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.03. Half volume (12.5 M tokens, first pass at minute 45, 13 passes, pages kept 37 minutes): today 2.71 / 3.74 / 3.14 s; b whole chain 2.34 / 2.43 / 2.43; b past the first prompt 0.70 / 0.83 / 0.64; c 0.29 / 0.29 / 0.32; three classes plus c 0.06 / 0.05 / 0.06. Quarter (6.2 M tokens, first pass at minute 24, 37 passes, pages kept 12 to 19 minutes): today 8.78 / 8.72 / 8.04 s (4.1 M tokens, 177 requests in ec_full); b whole chain 3.91 / 4.30 / 3.31; b past the first prompt 5.38 / 5.98 / 4.76; c 2.44 / 2.68 / 2.45; three classes plus c 0.87 / 0.98 / 0.74; with reference counts 0.46 / 0.41 / 0.40; oracle 0. Live pages deleted before 6,600 s by today's order: 7,038 at the run's volume, 26,683 at half, 121,935 at a quarter (ec_full). At a quarter 171 of 490 losing requests lose a head the session wrote itself (5.4 M of 10.7 M tokens); at the run's volume none do.
findings.method: compare.py <arm> 0.5|0.25 0.90 0.80 and 1.0 0.80 0.70 -> out/cmp_*.txt, out/compare_*.json; summary.py -> out/summary.txt; mechanisms.py -> out/mechanisms_ec_full_s0.5_90_80.txt, _s0.25_90_80.txt.
findings.implication: The loss grows quickly with a smaller volume or a longer run relative to the volume, and c alone stops being enough: the end signal's classes are needed so that idle open sessions outlive ended ones. These settings stretch the open-loop assumption most: the extra recompute would slow the box and change the timeline.

findings.question: Step 4: which mechanism does each loss come from, and which of b, c, d removes it?
findings.answer: ec_full, first pass to 6,600 s, requests / K tokens. (1) Shared head deleted (lookup finds nothing; the page was last written by another session): today 41 / 845; b whole chain 17 / 388 plus the partial chains below; b past the first prompt 0; c 3 / 22 (first requests only); three classes plus c 0. (2) Own head deleted (the session wrote it and is still open): 0 at the run's volume, 20 / 735 at half, 171 / 5,406 at a quarter; c alone leaves 55 / 1,531 at a quarter; three classes plus c 0. (3) Partial chain (a run of pages, then a hole): today 9 / 119, the hole being older than the pages before it because fix 1 touched the first pages again when someone recomputed them; b whole chain 102 / 1,857 (zero-time files deleted in scan order); b past the first prompt 6 / 89; c 3 / 44; d 1 / 0.8. (4) File deleted under a parked read: today 9 / 260; late in the run a read is done a median 39 s after its lookup (p90 52 s) and one missing file fails its 128-page batch and every later batch; c 0 at the run's volume and 4 at a quarter; a touch on lookup hits plus the re-check before unlink 0 at every volume.
findings.method: mechanisms.py (first deleted page met by a request's lookups or reads; writer and sharing per page) -> out/mechanisms_*.txt; look2.py for the lookup-to-read delay; cache_controller.py:1061-1076, 1103-1147 for the batch rule.
findings.implication: At the run's volume all four trace back to pages another session wrote, so c removes them; b is needed for mechanism 2, which appears only when the volume is small relative to session lifetimes, and it must stop at the first prompt or it manufactures mechanism 3.

findings.question: Is there any loss that only an in-memory index of stored pages would remove?
findings.answer: None found. With file times alone (three classes plus c) the remainder after the first pass is 0.8 K tokens at the run's volume, 110 K at half and 841 K at a quarter (ec_full). Reference counts over open sessions' chains, which the next-turn planner's per-session keys already imply, plus a touch on lookup hits and a re-check before unlink bring that to 0.8 K, 75 K and 547 K, and reads in flight to zero. Of the 547 K, 442 K (89 of 122 requests) are first requests of new sessions and the rest are later turns that pick up pages an ended session wrote: in both cases the last holder had ended before the user arrived. A use count per stored head page, which is what a page index could add, changed this by 3 % or less (532 against 547 K; equal at half and at the run's volume); keeping heads that two sessions had used out of the demoted class made it slightly worse (570 K).
findings.method: tier_count.py -> out/tier_count_*.txt; losses.py -> out/losses_ec_full_s0.25_tier_index.txt; compare.py orders d_tier_index+refresh+hit+recheck, d_tier_shared+refresh+hit+recheck.
findings.implication: Do not build the index for the cleaner's sake. Its other uses (lookups without a filesystem round trip, lookups for text no tier holds) were not tested here. The remaining loss needs foresight of sessions not yet arrived, or more volume.

findings.question: Is the SSD-tier change worth building, and how large is the gain?
findings.answer: Yes, and it is small code. At the run's setting the cleaner starts at minute 88 and costs 1.6 to 1.9 s of mean TTFT by N g from then on (0.77 to 0.90 M tokens per 20 minutes), in a service that runs past minute 88 for as long as it runs; at half the volume 2.7 to 3.7 s, at a quarter 8.0 to 8.8 s. A touch on lookup hits alone removes 95 to 97 % of it at the run's volume; the three classes with a refresh every 300 s per session remove 98 % or more at the run's and half volumes and about 90 % at a quarter. Seams: touch in hicache_nixl.py batch_exists (645-664) with touch_if_stored (nixl_utils.py:320-333); the end signal where next_turn_prefetch.py sets due = 'ended' (1526); the re-check in nixl_cleaner.py _safe_unlink (67-78), which already stats the file.
findings.method: Numbers from out/summary.txt and out/cmp_*.txt; seams read in the engine at HEAD.
findings.implication: Not established: the closed-loop effect and run-to-run spread, the cost of 430 to 1,900 utime calls a second on this filesystem, behaviour with more host memory (touch on read would protect less), whether end signals are reliable outside the replay (566 of 695 sessions send one here and it is exact), and real harnesses that re-send outputs (15 % of pages written here are outputs that no prompt uses).

surprises: 'Ended sessions' chains first' makes the SSD tier worse than today: 3.6 to 4.0 s against 1.6 to 1.9 s. 60 % of the shared tokens that new sessions find (1.38 of 2.30 M) were held only by sessions already over, and 94.5 % of cross-session sharing is in first prompts.
Touch on read alone removes 95 to 97 % of today's loss at the run's volume (0.07 to 0.08 s left), against the 23 November review's verdict that it would not protect shared heads.
The oracle loses nothing even at a quarter of the volume: open sessions' latest chains are 3.9 M tokens of 22.6 M stored, so the cleaner never needs to delete a live page.
Touching the head last so that tails are older than heads has no measurable effect (6 against 7 requests; 0.6 % of tokens at a quarter volume). What matters is that a refresh covers the whole chain.
A pass spends about 93 % of its 11 s scanning; the unlinks come in the last second. Lookups made up to 0.90 of the way through a pass still found files the pass then deleted under the parked read.
One deleted file fails a whole 128-page read batch and every later batch, and late in the run a read runs a median 39 s after its lookup, so 10 reads in ec_full lost up to 51 K tokens each.
23 of the 59 requests that lose history after the first pass are first requests of new sessions, which the earlier scripts (returning requests only) did not see; they are 12 % of the tokens.
jit_exact's client records carry no end flag (exact hints send no hint after the last request), so the end signal has to be taken from the trace for that arm.
An index's per-page use count and a refresh that rewrites missing pages both came out null.
